09bb5323109495b5: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 20 — The East Coast Rail Link (ECRL) will offer a 30 per cent discount on Economy Transit and Express fares for the first month of operations.

The Malaysia Rail Link Sdn Bhd (MRL) is targeting December 12 for the start of services, with ticket sales expected to begin in mid-November, Transport Minister Anthony Loke said after launching the Transport Expo Asia 2026 here today.

“The promotional discount applies to the public who do not qualify for existing concessionary fares, while eligible passengers, including persons with disabilities (OKU), children age two to 12, senior citizens and students, will continue to enjoy permanent 50 per cent discounts.
“Fares were set with affordability and the company’s financial sustainability in mind.
“We have taken a middle-ground approach,” Loke said, adding that while ECRL fares were comparable with airline tickets, they were significantly cheaper.

“Freight services connecting to Port Klang will take approximately another year to be completed, as construction of the section between Gombak and Port Klang is still ongoing.
“MRL will review freight charges in due course,” he added.
Cabinet approval on ECRL extension to Rantau Panjang
On the ECRL extension, Loke said the Cabinet has approved a proposed 32km extension Kota Bharu to Rantau Panjang, reaching the Malaysia-Thailand border.
“The project is now at the stage of cost and technical studies, alongside land acquisition, and is expected to take approximately four and a half years to complete.

“The first two years will focus mainly on land acquisition and technical evaluation, as land along the proposed corridor must be acquired from the state government and local landowners before construction can begin,” he said.

19b0c8a6f51c7c71: A website registered by “David Beckham” was the world’s second-most-visited source of pirated Japanese manga in February 2025, leading publishers to call for better verification of who buys domain names to address the problem.

The “Beckham” who registered the site was of course not the famous footballer and spokesmodel. However Tatsuo Ninoseki, an attorney with the Shin Hirakawa-Cho Law Office who represents the Japan Publishers manga Anti-Piracy Conference (JPMAC), put fake Becks in play today during a session on DNS abuse at ICANN’s annual meeting in Bali, Indonesia.

Ninoseki said miscreants routinely create unauthorized English translations of manga and post them on websites that include ads. The lawyer said such sites can attract hundreds of millions of users and cost publishers $17 billion in revenue each year.

JPMAC has decided its best course of action is not to pursue copyright abusers, but instead to go after commercial-scale pirates. That means it tries to act against pirate websites like those registered by “Beckham,” by sending them stern legal letters and using other legal means.

But those pirates have trained to get around defenders. Ninoseki said pirate manga sites maintain a set of domain names – he said they’ve registered names in 158 top-level domains and frequently “domain hop” between them.

The pirates’ pools of domains include some common naming elements, so even though Google has stopped indexing these pirate sites, users figure out that a theoretical piratemanga.XXX site will soon reappear at piratemanga.YYY.

Pirate sites also redirect from domains they’re not using to host content to another that is full of pirated comics. Sometimes they use several sites at once and direct users across a fleet of live sites, so traffic flows to each site stay small and don’t cause suspicion.

Ninoseki said 82.4 percent of domain hops happen within 15 days of the last move, suggesting pirates know how long enforcement actions or takedown requests will take and move to a different site before they run into trouble.
“Many domain hops do not appear to be a reaction to legal countermeasures,” the attorney said.

Ninoseki said JPMAC feels more comprehensive verification of domain name registrants would be a big help, especially checking physical addresses provided by registrants which he feels would weed out more pirates.
The lawyer spoke during an ICANN session on DNS abuse, which the governance body defines as using domain names to facilitate malware, botnets, phishing, pharming, and spam.

ICANN is currently working on a policy called PDP1 to address DNS abuse, one element of which would require registries to consider all domains held by their customers if just one is found to conduct DNS abuse. That policy would mean that once a registrant named “David Beckham” is connected to a single piracy site, all other domains registered by fake Becks would be checked in case they’re also committing DNS fouls. ®

7a9898c01ede12be: If Bersama were to contest 15 seats in the Melaka polls on Nov 14, it is certain to take away votes from PKR, DAP and Amanah.

It is not too late to rescind a move that bodes ill for a future in which Bersama ought to have a vital role in making the reforms long sought by Pakatan Harapan (PH) a reality, thereby setting on course the creation of a different country from the prevailing one, whose contours are likely to be reinforced by the right-wingers of Umno and the Islamists of PAS.

As if the good fairies have decided to play a hand in steering things towards an outcome both congenial for Bersama and beneficial to PH, Bersama’s co-founder Nik Nazmi Nik Ahmad is in a spot of bother that may well throw him off stride for GE16.

The khalwat case he is facing may well disqualify the former MP for Setiawangsa from being the constituency’s first Bersama MP at GE16. Prior to the case’s inception, Nik Nazmi was on course, after resigning as PKR MP for Setiawangsa, to being returned at GE16, under Bersama’s colours, as the seat’s MP.
Now that probability is dimmed by what hangs over him at the shariah court.

This is grist for the argument that Bersama ought to draw in its tentacles and play to its strengths. There is no point in splitting votes at the Melaka polls and persisting in attacking PKR and Anwar Ibrahim on the stumps, as Bersama has been known to do from the time the party set sail.

When Rafizi Ramli and Nik Nazmi launched a new political vehicle by forming Bersama, it was clear the pair were on course, heading up to GE16, which must be called by February 2028, to carve off something like 10 of the 31 parliamentary seats that PKR won at GE15 in November 2022.
Their incumbents were pro-Rafizi and will likely be won again by the same coterie if re-contested by them.
Bersama will want to contest a number of other seats held by PKR MPs, but not significantly more.

Bersama went into the Johor state polls in July with hopes of making some gains. They wound up with nothing but lost deposits and were suitably chagrined to not want to contest in the subsequent Negeri Sembilan polls.
But now Bersama fancies its chances in Melaka: it has not learnt its lesson that what plays in the Klang Valley does not exactly play outside its highly urban and urbane precincts.
The Nik Nazmi khalwat case is a symptom of Bersama’s presumptuousness.
The party must play within its strengths.
And wait for the realisation to congeal that after Anwar, it is Rafizi who should resuscitate the fallen reformasi colours.
Hence, there isn’t much point in alienating its putative allies in PKR, DAP and Amanah by going solo and splitting votes at the Melaka polls and elsewhere.
What has happened to Nik Nazmi should introduce some grains of sand into Bersama’s balm of complacent assumption.
Terence Netto is a senior journalist and an FMT reader.

394cca3f8c173049: ICANN has started testing authentication schemes that will allow law enforcement agencies to make urgent requests for non-public WHOIS information – when needed to address threats to life, critical infrastructure, or child exploitation.

Domain registrars collect information about their customers and in the past that data was publicly available in WHOIS records. Some domain registrars offer services that substitute their own contact details, to preserve customer privacy. In recent years, laws like GDPR mean registrars are sometimes required to hide WHOIS data.

That’s fair enough but makes it hard for law enforcement to contact a domain holder if their resources are being misused – intentionally or otherwise – for purposes such as hosting malware, acting as command-and-control infrastructure for malware, or facilitating phishing.

ICANN’s definition for the kind of behaviour it thinks justifies urgent requests for WHOIS info is “imminent threat to life, of serious bodily injury, to critical infrastructure, or of child exploitation.”

The org has convened an Input Group on Law Enforcement Agency Authentication Mechanisms to consider the issue, and that group yesterday explained its progress during ICANN’s annual meeting in Bali, Indonesia.
At this point, readers may have concerns that this proposal could allow law enforcement authorities to make inappropriate requests for WHOIS information.
Several factors may ease such concerns.
One is that representatives of domain registrars Namecheap and Verisign spoke during the session about the proposal, and both were supportive.

Another is that the Input Group’s work is largely technical. Once it devises a mechanism to allow requests, other groups within ICANN dedicated to policy will work out acceptable use and related issues.

This is the way internet governance gets done! Specialists work on their own bits of a problem and then collaborate to create a robust system that works at a technical level, is practical, and enforceable in multiple jurisdictions.

At this point, ICANN’s preferred approach is to use Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) so that authenticated users at law enforcement agencies can log into the governance org’s Registration Data Request Service (RDRS) and file requests to access non-public WHOIS info. ICANN is already testing this approach with the FBI and Interpol but is open to other authentication mechanisms to allow other agencies access RDRS. The Input Group’s aim is to publish a spec those agencies can conform to.

ICANN will pass requests filed in RDRS to whichever registrar sold the domain. The registrar will have 24 hours to consider the request – or up to 72 hours for complex queries. Registrars will also be able to deny requests if they feel the query does not meet the urgency threshold.
Register readers might worry that a colossal agency like the FBI could flood RDRS with requests from thousands of individual agents, swamping domain registries.

ICANN’s plan is to avoid that by requiring law enforcement agencies to nominate certain personnel who are permitted to make requests, and to enforce that permission using a token shared during SAML handshakes. The content of that token is the kind of policy question that the Input Group expects others at ICANN to finalize later.

Another issue under consideration is how to protect the identity of law enforcement workers who make RDRS requests, as ICANN feels they could become targets of harassment (or worse) if their requests to see WHOIS data include email addresses. ®

6c941b9db65caba4: Hidup berjiran memang ada macam-macam ragam.

Ada jiran yang baik hati, suka menolong, ringan tulang dan mengambil berat tentang orang sekeliling. Ada juga jiran yang kita tidak begitu kenal, tetapi tidak pernah mendatangkan masalah. Masing-masing menjaga hal sendiri.
Ada yang sudah bertahun-tahun tinggal berdepan-depan, tetapi sekadar angkat tangan dan senyum. Tidak pernah berbual. Janji tidak menyusahkan orang lain, kita baik-baik sahaja.
Ada juga yang langsung tidak mahu memandang, apatah lagi bertegur sapa. Tetapi selagi tidak membuat susah kepada orang lain, itu pun tidak mengapa.
Yang susah apabila mendapat jiran yang selalu buat hal. Entah apa penyakitnya, suka membuat orang lain tidak senang.
Laman rumahnya bersemak-samun sehingga mungkin menjadi tempat pembiakan nyamuk. Ditambah pula suka membuat bising tidak mengenal waktu. Sudah tentu kita semua akan rimas dan serba salah.
Apabila ditegur, dia tidak berubah. Silap-silap kita pula diajak bertumbuk.

Bukan dia sahaja yang menyusahkan, seluruh keluarganya pun sama. Anak-anak bukan main nakal, suka mengganggu rakan sebaya. Emaknya pula bermulut jahat, suka mengata sana-sini. Tidak boleh tengok orang lain lebih sedikit, dinaikkan pula hantaran menyindir di media sosial.

Lama-kelamaan, seluruh kejiranan bengang dan terganggu dengan perangai jiran seperti ini sehingga masalah itu terpaksa dibawa ke mesyuarat persatuan penduduk, malah memerlukan campur tangan ketua masyarakat atau pihak berkuasa.
Tetapi masalah tetap tidak selesai. Dia masih tidak berubah.
Apabila ada pihak datang sebagai wakil pendamai untuk memujuk, pandai pula dia mengajar orang lain. Disuruhnya kita bersabar. Katanya, hidup berjiran perlu ada toleransi.

Kemudian dia merengek dan berlakon menjadi mangsa. Orang lain semuanya salah, dia sahaja yang betul. Disebut-sebut dan diungkit-ungkit pula apa yang sudah dilakukannya selama ini. Kononnya dia juga ada jasa di kawasan kejiranan.
Ini bukan cerita rekaan.
Kalau kita tinggal di kampung, rumah pangsa rakyat atau taman perumahan, memang ada orang jenis begini. Kadang-kadang kita pun tidak faham bagaimana orang seperti mereka boleh wujud di muka bumi ini.
Ketika orang lain sepakat dan boleh hidup aman, dia muncul mengocak ketenangan. Apa kepuasan yang dia dapat, kita pun tidak boleh hendak hadam.
Takkanlah tidak tahu bahawa dalam beragama memang ada bab adab hidup berjiran. Kita dituntut supaya menghormati jiran, menjaga hubungan baik dan tidak menyusahkan orang lain.

Tetapi hubungan baik sepatutnya berjalan dua hala. Tidak bolehlah seorang jiran sentiasa diminta bersabar sedangkan jiran yang menyebabkan masalah sewenang-wenangnya melakukan apa sahaja yang dia suka.
Hal-hal mudah pun sepatutnya kita boleh fikir sendiri.
Jangan halang pintu keluar masuk rumah jiran dengan kereta kita. Jangan biarkan haiwan peliharaan membuang najis merata-rata di atas jalan atau di rumah jiran.
Pada musim perayaan, kalau boleh elakkan membakar mercun apabila sudah masuk waktu tidur. Ada anak kecil dan orang tua yang tidak sihat, pasti mereka akan terkejut.
Jangan pula bakar sampah sehingga asap masuk ke rumah jiran.
Ini semua perkara yang kita boleh fikir sendiri.
Tetapi nanti sekejap.
Bagaimana kalau mereka sebenarnya tahu perbuatan itu menyusahkan orang lain, tetapi tidak mempedulikannya?
Lebih teruk lagi jika mereka mendapat keuntungan daripada perbuatan itu, sedangkan orang lain terpaksa menanggung akibatnya.
Ini bukan lagi soal kesedaran atau common sense. Ini sudah masuk soal tanggungjawab.
Rasulullah SAW bersabda, maksudnya:
“Demi Allah, tidak beriman! Demi Allah, tidak beriman! Demi Allah, tidak beriman!”
Apabila ditanya siapakah orang itu, Baginda menjawab:
“Orang yang jirannya tidak berasa aman daripada gangguannya.”
(Riwayat al-Bukhari, no. 6016)

Apabila dikatakan jiran, ia jelas tidak terbatas kepada kaum dan agama. Jiran ialah mereka yang paling dekat di sekeliling kita, yang bersama-sama menjadi sebahagian daripada sesebuah kelompok atau komuniti.
Begitulah Islam mementingkan kesejahteraan jiran tetangga. Kita dituntut berbuat baik kepada jiran walaupun berbeza warna kulit dan kepercayaan.
Tetapi watak pengacau tetap ada.
Bukan di rumah sahaja. Di dalam bilik darjah, pasti ada seorang watak pengacau atau kaki buli. Di pejabat pula ada kaki mengadu domba.
Malah, di peringkat dunia pun ada negara yang kita panggil jiran tetapi suka buat hal.
Tiap-tiap tahun rumah kita dimasuki asap gara-gara jiran membuat pembakaran “di halamannya”. Kita dan jiran-jiran lain sudah puas mengeluh, tetapi dia tidak peduli.
Apa kita hendak buat dengan mereka?
Sikap tidak mempedulikan pihak lain ini cukup membuatkan kita tertekan. Kita bingung dan mati kutu. Sampai bilakah keadaan ini akan berterusan? Bilakah pula mereka akan sedar dan berubah?
Maka, setelah puas mengeluh, ayuhlah kita berdoa kepada tuhan agar pintu akal mereka terbuka dan mereka menjadi lebih bijak sedikit.
Berdoalah sungguh-sungguh sebelum terlambat. Sebelum keamanan dan kesihatan kita musnah.
Bukan apa.
Saya sudah bosan dengan jerebu ini.
Tolonglah, wahai jiran!
Bebaskan kami daripada kekaburan yang melemaskan paru-paru ini.
Kami semakin tidak tahan!

773c6020d7b35831: From Moaz Nair
Not too long ago, Negeri Sembilan stood proud as a bastion of political tranquillity amidst a turbulent national landscape.

Under the previous Barisan Nasional–Pakatan Harapan coalition government led by former menteri besar Aminuddin Harun, the state enjoyed a rare commodity in modern Malaysian politics: absolute administrative stability.

Today, that hard-won stability has been recklessly squandered. Negeri Sembilan now finds itself ensnared in a historic, multi-layered constitutional crisis born entirely of the current government’s own missteps.

For the voters, legal experts, and everyday citizens witnessing this paralysis, the contrast between past order and present dysfunction could not be starker. The memory of the previous BN-PH framework is fast becoming the definitive benchmark for stable governance and a bitter reminder of how far the state has fallen.

The crowning achievement of the previous administration was its meticulous commitment to preserving constitutional harmony and institutional traditions. Negeri Sembilan’s governance model is uniquely complex, relying on a centuries-old, delicate equilibrium between a modern elected executive, the monarchy, and the state’s sacred, uncodified Adat Perpatih (customary law) institutions.

Aminuddin’s government managed this sensitive balance not by luck, but through sheer political maturity and institutional restraint. Recognising the vital need to insulate daily partisan politics from royal affairs, his government maintained a peaceful, respectful coexistence between elected officials, the Undang Yang Empat (traditional chieftains), and the Yang Dipertuan Besar.
Mutual respect
It was a partnership built on mutual respect and systemic boundaries, ensuring that time-honoured traditions and modern democracy reinforced rather than undermined one another.

Crucially, this political maturity served as a protective shield that insulated the state from systemic crises. Backers of the previous government frequently note that the coalition successfully shielded the civil service and state apparatus from being dragged into protracted constitutional disputes.

Today, we realise just how vital that bulwark was, and how easily it could be dismantled by naked political opportunism. The moment the BN-PH cooperation fractured, it triggered an unprecedented and destructive chain reaction that has shaken the state to its core.

The descent into absolute turmoil accelerated rapidly last April, when 14 BN assemblymen abruptly withdrew their support from Aminuddin’s government following a dispute involving royal affairs. Rather than prioritising state stability, this drastic move plunged the state into a perilous political vacuum, leaving a minority government in its wake and forcing a snap election.

This vacuum did more than just disrupt daily executive governance; it threw open the doors to the current existential crisis— an unprecedented, overt succession dispute between Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir and Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja’afar, who is backed by the current administration.
Constitutional deadlock
The collapse of the foundational political consensus has dragged the state legislative assembly into a complex, multi-layered constitutional deadlock with no clear legal exit ramp.

We are now forced to witness an extraordinary and embarrassing clash of powers. In direct response to aggressive moves by the new state executive council supporting a proclamation to depose him, Tuanku Muhriz took the radical but decisive step of revoking the appointments of all 10 state executive councillors. Citing a direct breach of their oaths of office, the palace purged the state cabinet in one swift stroke.

The fallout has left governance not just shaky, but completely paralysed. The current menteri besar, Ismail Lasim, now stands isolated—a lone captain aboard a ghost ship. In a bizarre attempt to downplay this structural damage, Ismail has chosen to prioritise appointing village chiefs and village development and security committees rather than resolving the critical vacancies in his cabinet.

To claim that state administration is "running smoothly" while the formal sitting of the state assembly has been indefinitely postponed until late November is an insult to the voters' intelligence. This represents a profound failure of the democratic apparatus, where grassroots local appointments are being deployed as a smoke screen to mask a total absence of executive authority.
Painful lesson

Negeri Sembilan is learning a painful lesson first-hand: when you dismantle a functional political consensus for short-term gain, the alternative is rarely better. The current turmoil proves that the previous BN-PH ruling alliance was not merely a marriage of convenience — it was a vital stabilising force.

The current menteri besar cannot continue to govern in a state of absolute paralysis, pretending that village-level appointments can substitute for a functioning state legislative assembly or a complete Exco line-up.

The state’s political leaders must urgently put aside partisan egos, halt their dangerous chess game against traditional institutions, and return to the constitutional blueprint that guaranteed peace for years. The state's executive vacuum is no longer an isolated political squabble; it is a systemic crisis threatening the very fabric of Negeri Sembilan’s unique identity.
If the current leadership is incapable of restoring the stable, respectful equilibrium of the past, they must accept their failure and step aside for those who can.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

5284103de5a2389c: The US Department of Homeland Security on Monday issued an order directing federal civilian agencies not to use technology products from Chinese AI lab DeepSeek, and to remove any existing implementations.
The order [PDF] is broad, as it requires agencies to ditch "all DeepSeek and DeepSeek-affiliate products, and third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations."

Complying will be tricky as it is not clear which third-party products and services have been developed using DeepSeek's wares. Nor is it clear whether "developed using" means providing ongoing access to DeepSeek models via API or simply refers to any app vibe-coded with the help of DeepSeek.

It also leaves open the question of AI gateways. Services such as OpenRouter and Vercel AI Gateway make DeepSeek's models available through APIs. And those using gateway services may find themselves using DeepSeek models without meaning to do so.

OpenRouter, for example, "routes requests to the best available providers for your model." It selects what the service deems to be the best fit provider of AI services. Vercel AI Gateway does the same by default. So federal civilian agencies could be using DeepSeek models inadvertently, if they haven't taken steps to constrain their AI providers.
A DHS spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

US officials have contemplated a ban on DeepSeek since the China-based AI lab released DeepSeek-R1 in early 2025. On February 6, 2025, US Representative Darin LaHood (R-IL) and US Representative Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ) introduced the No DeepSeek on Government Devices Act. The lawmakers characterised DeepSeek as a national security threat because its AI models purportedly capture data on US citizens and provide it to the Chinese government. The bill never made it out of committee, but various government agencies followed through.

The US Defense community and lawmakers have already exiled DeepSeek. The Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) started blocking DeepSeek on the Pentagon’s IT networks in January 2025. The US Navy, NASA, and the US House of Representatives took similar steps. So did various US states.

While the DHS announcement has taken a long time to reach civilian agencies, its timing may be a boon for American AI companies which, like Anthropic, hope to soon go public. That's because open weight models represent competition, and those from China have proven particularly popular both in terms of capabilities and cost. Government agencies that cannot deploy such models (and the taxpayers who fund those agencies) may be stuck paying the prices set by favored US model makers.

Concerns about the security and privacy of DeepSeek's iOS mobile app surfaced shortly after DeepSeek-R1 debuted. Several months later, a December 2025 report on the DeekSeek mobile app for Android and iOS cited similar concerns, including plaintext information leaks, links to servers run by Chinese tech firms, and shortcomings like lack of SSL pinning.

These issues, however, are mainly mobile security problems that afflict many apps, particularly those that integrate third-party advertising SDKs from companies based outside the US. They don't really address the additional risks posed by the capture of text prompts and responses, or how local secrets and other sensitive information can be ingested by AI agents.

Katie Moussouris, founder and CEO of Luta Security, told The Register in an email that while there are legitimate national security reasons to keep DeepSeek's app and servers away from government systems, the way this particular order is written exceeds that requirement in ways that aren't practical.

"Banning DeepSeek's own app and API is workable," said Moussouris. "The problem is the ban on 'third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations.' The order doesn't say what 'developed using' means. It could technically cover any model derived from DeepSeek and more importantly, any software whose developers used DeepSeek to write or test code. An AI software bill of materials doesn't record which tools developers used, so it would be no real help. Every vendor would have to attest that nothing it relies on ever touched DeepSeek. There's no practical way to verify that."
Moussouris also took issue with the breadth of the order, noting that applying the rules to US-hosted versions of DeepSeek's models goes too far.
"The risks the order cites are mostly about data flowing to DeepSeek's servers in China, its data collection, and its app," she said. "US hosting avoids most of those.

"For the model itself, the order says only that it may contain malware or vulnerabilities, which is true of all software. NIST found DeepSeek more vulnerable to prompt injection than US models, though every model has that problem. NIST also found it easier to jailbreak, but jailbreak guardrails often get in the way of defenders." ®

5896ab894451fee5: Over the Merdeka holidays, I went fishing with some friends off the Pahang and Johor coast. We started off from the Kuala Rompin jetties on a lovely morning with mist shrouding the mangrove and hovering over the river. It was a beautiful, peaceful sight.

Then the sun started getting hotter but the mist remained… and remained, acting in a most un-misty way. When we sailed away from the river mouth we could still see this “mist” all around us. It wasn’t mist. It was the haze, right there on the east coast hundreds of kilometres from the nearest Indonesian territories, yet enough of it was visible even in Pulau Tioman.

Over the last few months, I've been saying “I've never seen haze this bad, only to update it again multiple times on subsequent days. The haze last week was especially bad, but I’m sure as records go this too will be broken soon.

What can I say about the haze that hasn’t been said by many for years? I’m relatively healthy for my age and don’t have any bad allergy problems, but I still get headaches and nausea because of it. I can’t bear to think about what those with actual health issues must be going through.
The current haze seems worse than previous ones. It hangs heavy and feels thick and foul, often covering the sun and hills and gloomily blocking vision to barely a kilometre or so on the highway.

Everybody is frustrated with it, including an Indonesian official who slammed his Malaysian and Singaporean neighbours for complaining about the haze from Sumatra without acknowledging it also gives us oxygen during better days.

Hello! Our Indonesian official friend forgets his high school chemistry. Sumatra is passing us more than oxygen now, this time the said oxygen is all bound up with carbon and sulphur and nitrogen and other elements to form noxious and poisonous monoxides and dioxides and ozone!
Not exactly the kind of trade among friends. After decades of “importing” this stuff for months most years, we deserve a breather, if you’ll pardon the expression.
The Indonesians are also experimenting with clearing the haze with dry ice, which is supposed to lift the smoke particles higher into the atmosphere and clear the land.

Great – now the smoke particles will go even higher into the Indonesian skies to catch the stronger monsoon wind up there and even more of them can waft their way to Malaysia. Thank you again Indonesia!

In reality, Indonesia’s forest fire problem has gotten out of hand. The fires have literally gone underground, setting off the uncontrollable burning of dry underground peat. Once this catches fire, only the deluge of a monsoon can put it out.

This year a combination of factors, including a more severe El Nino, is exacerbating the problem; perhaps a madder-than-usual rush to burn forests, because there’s less of them left every year, is making things worse.

What we need to see is a more aggressive attitude among the political leaders of the region in fighting this menace. Our own leaders must also start demanding more be done by Indonesia to stop this perennial curse.

Of the culprits setting the forest on fire in Sumatra and Kalimantan are believed to include some big Malaysian plantation companies. If that is so, bring them to account and throw the book at them: I can guarantee there’ll be loud cheers from us ordinary Malaysians.
And ordinary Indonesians too. If it’s bad for us hundreds of kilometres away from the worst of it, just imagine how bad it must be for the unfortunate people living right there.

They can't go fishing away from the haze, like I did. They can’t get into private jets and fly out of the country to foreign clearer skies, as some people did. They just have to stay there and suck it all in literally and suffer now and/or die earlier later.

Our problems are not with the ordinary Indonesians, many of whom suffer even worse than us because of this haze. Our issues are with the Indonesian authorities who we don’t see treating the problem as the emergency it actually is.
And our issue is also with our own leaders who are more interested in maintaining peace and harmony while our people are literally choking with illness and maybe even death.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

47a60e4c73371f7c: Dutch grocery giant Ahold Delhaize, which operates US supermarket chains Food Lion, Giant Food, and Stop & Shop, said it proactively took IT systems offline following a cyberattack, affecting most of its US and European brands.

The multinational chain originally disclosed the incident on October 12. “Ahold Delhaize is experiencing a security issue within its network,” it said at the time, adding that security teams, working to mitigate the issues, took “some” IT systems offline.

On Monday, the company confirmed that it proactively took certain IT systems, including websites and apps, offline, affecting most of its brands, and said that “malicious actions of others” caused the security issue.

“Taking systems offline to help protect them was a precautionary measure that affected most of our brands across Europe and the United States,” Frans Muller, president and CEO of Ahold Delhaize, said in a Monday statement. “The investigation to date confirms this was the right decision.”

At this time, all of the physical stores remain open, and the investigation hasn’t uncovered any evidence to suggest the miscreants stole any “sensitive customer, associate, or partner data,” the disclosure said.
The company last week notified the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre about the digital intruders, and on Monday filed a report with the Dutch police, according to the statement.

Albert Heijn’s website and app are back online, and the company expects home deliveries to resume on Friday. Belgian e-commerce is fully operational, and e-commerce services at Ahold Delhaize’s American brands (Food Lion, Giant Food, Martin’s, Hannaford, and Stop & Shop) are expected to work “in the coming days.”
The Etos and Gall & Gall websites are also up and running, along with the “majority of websites and apps” across brands serving central and southeastern Europe.

Ahold Delhaize did not immediately respond to The Register’s questions about the cyberattack, including whether it was linked to attacks on refrigeration controllers at hundreds of French supermarkets beginning October 11. The attacks reportedly pushed temperatures as high as 122°F (50°C), spoiling food and causing fires at some locations.

This latest cyberattack is Ahold Delhaize’s second in two years. A November 2024 digital break-in disrupted brands across the organization, with some Stop & Shop stores struggling to fill prescriptions, while Food Lion employees reported delayed and missing deliveries.
INC Ransom claimed responsibility for the attack at the time and leaked some documents reportedly taken from the retailer's systems.
Ahold Delhaize ultimately determined more than 2.2 million people’s data - including personal, financial, and health details - had been compromised. ®
e5eadce826998ef4: To feed its Indiana datacenters with plenty of juice, Amazon is funding the development of a new nuclear facility that will provide nearly 1 gigawatt of power. However, we'll have to see if this happens anytime soon, given the immature technology it's using.

Amazon said on Monday that it was funding the project with an undisclosed amount of cash as part of an expansion of its existing deal with X-energy, a next-generation nuclear power startup focusing on building small modular reactors (SMRs) powered by Tri-Structural ISOtropic (TRISO) fuel pellets and cooled by helium gas.
Amazon would tell us only that it’s “investing billions in nuclear energy projects” without getting specific on this project.

According to X-energy, the project will see Amazon fund the development of 12 of those SMRs, its Xe-100 model, in Sullivan County, Indiana, at the site of a former coal power plant. Once up and running, the facility will supply 960 megawatts of grid-connected electricity, with Amazon contracting as the first power purchaser from the future plant.

As for when it might come online, that’s anyone’s guess. Amazon wouldn’t tell us, only pointing us to an article in Indiana newspaper the South Bend Tribune in which an X-energy representative said it could be completed “as early as the mid-2030s,” though “the timeline could change the further the project gets developed.”
That’s quite likely given X-energy’s current status and the state of next-generation nuclear power more generally, and to understand why it helps to understand how nuclear permitting works in the US.

First off, despite the promises, hype, and mountains of cash poured into nuclear power by the tech industry, the US has yet to build a single operable SMR. China and Russia have built functional SMRs. A single experimental unit has achieved criticality in the US, but it’s not a functional, power-producing reactor and was only built to demonstrate the ability for a specific design to become one. The company with that experimental US SMR is not X-energy, who has yet to build a working reactor.

As to how reactors get approved in the US, there are two pathways that nuclear power companies can pursue: One is to get a standard design approval from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC). That pathway gives a company license to build a reactor of a specific model wherever they want, as the design has been deemed safe independent of any physical site. That means the certified reactor can be sold and built without the need for the NRC to recertify the core design each time a project gets underway.

There is only one company in the US that has a standard design approval for an SMR: Nuscale, which has yet to build a single reactor, has no projects under construction, and has already abandoned a Utah plant due to lack of interest from power distributors.

The other option allows SMR developers to get approval for a site-specific project, which is quicker and involves the NRC blessing a particular reactor in a particular place. There have been several of those permits awarded, with Kairos Power being approved to build an SMR in Oak Ridge, Tennessee in partnership with Google, General Electric planning another SMR in Oak Ridge, and TerraPower inching forward with its own project in Wyoming despite delays.

Notice X-energy isn’t mentioned there, either. The company claims that it’s in “the final phases” of NRC approval for a construction permit in Texas, where it’ll supply power for a Dow Chemical manufacturing plant, but that likely won’t matter too much for the Indiana project’s timeline. As mentioned above, nuclear construction permits are site specific, and the Texas plant only involves four reactors - far fewer than the 12 planned in Indiana.
X-energy didn’t respond to questions for this story, but Amazon told us it's not going to be involved in any way with getting approval across the finish line for the Indiana plant.

“Amazon's role is as an investor … as well as committing to being the first customer for power produced from the facility,” a company spokesperson told us. “New technologies like this often need initial customers to help de-risk projects and provide funding so they can be built and scaled to commercial availability, and that is the role Amazon is playing by helping to fund the project's development.”
Like other large, ambitious next-generation nuclear projects, in other words, this one is just as much in the maybe column as the rest. ®

8b2c60ecf7a9eebf: The first order of business for the energy transition is electrifying applications like vehicles and heating and making sure that the electricity that powers them is made using renewables. But once the dominant slices of the emissions pie have shrunk, other categories with less potential to reduce emissions become important.

A new study led by Haiwei Zhou at the University of Melbourne focused on the emissions associated with making lithium-ion batteries, which many parts of the energy transition rely on. Those emissions aren’t zero, so as we use more and more batteries, that number will grow. Right now, the researchers estimate that these emissions only account for 0.18 percent of annual greenhouse gas releases, but they could increase by a factor of 10 or more by 2050.

There are a number of ways to reduce the emissions required to make a battery. Some elements used in various lithium-ion battery chemistries are more energy-intensive to mine and refine than others. The battery manufacturing process involves many steps that could be made more energy-efficient. And then there’s recycling, which can put battery materials back into the loop while requiring much less energy than mining.
3bf87038d3406f87: It may not be enough to just use LLMs to write your code when you can also use them to adjust it while your program runs. DoubleAI, a Tel Aviv, Israel-based startup founded in 2023, on Monday introduced Maxwell, a code execution model (CEM) that evaluates, optimizes, and rewrites binary code during execution.

Named for Maxwell's Demon, a creature imagined by physicist and mathematician James Clerk Maxwell in 1867 as part of a thought experiment on entropy, the Maxwell CEM preprocesses algorithms and machine instructions to maximize performance on available hardware.
Maxwell is similar in concept to a just-in-time compiler, but provides more flexibility and formally verifies the equivalence of replacement code. Source code isn't touched.

"Both Maxwell and a JIT compiler work while the program runs and both produce new machine code," said doubleAI co-founder Gal Beniamini, who holds a PhD in theoretical computer science, in an email to The Register. "The difference is that a compiler can't do high-level reasoning. It can't, for example, change the algorithm. Maxwell can and does.

"One of the reasons why JIT compilers are so narrow is that, even though they can be data-dependent, the changes they make must be deterministic and correct 'by construction,' since JIT compilers are 'unthinking' classical algorithms.

"Maxwell brings the expressive power of frontier AI into the 'JIT' setting. In addition, Maxwell relies on formal verification to write actual, hard proofs that show that its optimizations are sound. This expands the scope of its allowed optimisation far beyond that of any algorithm or compiler."
Beniamini pointed to sorting as an example. The compiler, he said, will make a general-purpose sorting algorithm run as fast as it can, but it won't swap it out for a different algorithm.
Compilers, said Beniamini, make decisions before the program runs and have to be narrow and conservative in their choices.
Maxwell, he said, works with more information, isn't just a one-pass operation, and operates at a higher level.

"It sees the exact hardware the program has landed on, and the actual shapes and types of the data flowing through it (information that is only available during runtime!)," Beniamini explained. "It also sees the state of the environment, what else is running in the same program, and which actual bottlenecks express themselves, and under which conditions. This allows it to specialize in ways a compiler never can."
Since Maxwell operates continuously, it can keep improving programs as new bottlenecks arise. And it can "reason" in a way that compilers cannot.
Maxwell's approach wouldn't be possible if the model rewrote code in a way that introduced errors on the fly, so the formal proof capability is not optional.
According to doubleAI, Maxwell has made data pipelines more than 38x faster and AI inference kernels more than 4.5x faster.

LTX-2.5, an open world model that generates 4K video, managed to do so almost twice as fast with the help of Maxwell. Maxwell's optimizations reduced the data being exchanged between GPUs and optimized the kernel selection to drop unnecessary token padding.
Maxwell's optimization capability varies depending on the source code and the hardware.

"Maxwell does best on code that is algorithmic, and which can be tailored to hardware in a non-trivial manner," said Beniamini. "That being said, even code that isn't like that, but is written in a high level language like Python, can usually enjoy far reaching optimisations due to the available overhang. The same is true for PyTorch graphs, which (even under Torch's compiler) tend to be extremely far from optimal."
It can also help with code security. Beniamini said Maxwell can eliminate issues like memory errors by proving their non-existence as part of the formalization process.
"Anecdotally, we have found such issues in Python itself, through the use of Maxwell – i.e., cases in which Python was not memory safe, and where Maxwell proved that to be the case," he said.
And better still, Maxwell's tracing and profiling don't incur much if any overhead on either the CPU or GPU.

"The maximal overhead of Maxwell's tracing and profiling is 2 percent (when it isn't tracing, that falls to zero, of course), and the optimisations that Maxwell yields far outweigh that," said Beniamini. "We also apply Maxwell to the runtime itself, so that we get back a much larger than 2 percent 'flat' speedup, across the board. So in short: it's never slower."

The installation process is similarly light-touch: Devs install the runtime and run their code, with the Maxwell model hosted by doubleAI. This arrangement, however, does require some amount of trust.

Amnon Shashua, co-founder and CEO of doubleAI, founder and departing CEO of Mobileye and a professor of computer science at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said in a statement that AI has changed how software is written and now is changing how it runs.

"CEMs, and Maxwell in particular, are agents on behalf of the hardware as opposed to code agents that are on behalf of the human user," he said. "In other words, they are the first AI that works for the machine, not the programmer." ®
6dcd14183fe24565: Recently fixed vulnerabilities in the Plex Media Server are under active exploitation in attacks that, when successful, install malware, including cryptominers and residential proxy apps, a researcher said.

Plex fixed four vulnerabilities at the start of last month. Three weeks later, published CVE designations revealed five vulnerabilities, with one of them carrying a severity rating of 8.6 out of 10. A researcher last week revealed an exploit that chained four of them together to achieve remote code execution of the device running a vulnerable Plex version. The researcher named the chain "Plex2Shell."

The new details allowed a separate researcher to create a honeypot that could track attempts in the wild to exploit the vulnerability chain. Within a day, the researcher began seeing active scanning of the simulated Plex server and eventually successful attempts to infect devices. So far, successful attacks are installing two payloads. One is a cryptominer, which uses the device to mine cryptocurrency and deposit it into a wallet controlled by the attacker. The other payload is residential proxy software, which allows people to anonymize their Internet activity (much of it illegal) by connecting to the infected box and then using it to send the user’s traffic to a final destination.
5fa54fa214dd1429: The world’s first demonstration of a subsea geothermal power plant has taken place near an active underwater volcano almost a mile below the ocean surface. 45e4ee4d23d59f17: Open source Windows alternative ReactOS has reached a major milestone: The operating system can now be installed directly onto an NT Files System drive partition. As reported by Phoronix, the move to NTFS clears a long-standing hurdle for the project and brings it one step closer to finally reaching beta.

Prior to this latest announcement, ReactOS required users to keep a FAT32 partition for installations. A proprietary Microsoft-developed filesystem, NTFS can trace its roots back through the Windows NT family lineage starting in 1993 with Windows NT 3.1. The variant introduced with Windows XP in 2001 remains the standard used by most Windows systems today. With ReactOS's stated goal of reaching binary compatibility with Windows Server 2003, being confined to FAT32 partitions was a practical barrier to clear on the way to reproducing the Windows environment.

However, users looking to hop off the Windows train shouldn't be grabbing their bags just yet. ReactOS wrote that the new driver still "lacks caching (which causes inferior performance), journaling and security support." So while the new driver is here, even the most intrepid of OS tinkerers should tread carefully. The ReactOS team warned in its announcement on X that there are still "potentially undiscovered bugs."
545214fd4da00ea0: Updating your software only gets you so far. A scary scenario - security fixes themselves being bypassed - is becoming more common, according to AI penetration-testing startup Terra Security, which found a sharp rise in reported patch failures in 2026 after years of relatively low numbers.
And no, it’s not a coincidence that AI vulnerability discovery and patching also exploded this year.

For example, Russian government cyberspies exploited a zero-day Windows Shell security bypass bug, CVE-2026-21510, at least a month before Microsoft patched the flaw in February. Redmond’s patch, however, was incomplete, and left a second flaw - a zero-click authentication coercion vulnerability (CVE-2026-32202) - that was also found and abused before Microsoft fixed it in April.

Terra researchers reviewed every published CVE record and GitHub-reviewed advisory looking for broken fixes, and found a distinct pattern. After six years of relatively few patch bypasses, this changed in 2026: “A fix would ship, a bypass would be found, and another fix would go out.”

The share of GitHub security fixes that required a follow-up advisory reporting a failed patch within 90 days remained at about 0.2 percent between 2019 and 2025. This year, this figure had jumped to 2.3 percent, according to the researchers.

Meanwhile, vulnerabilities whose fixes were later bypassed were about four times as likely to appear on the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA's) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list as other bugs affecting the same vendors, according to Terra.

Of these, server-side request forgery fixes and prototype-pollution patches break the most. Compared with their share of all CVEs, prototype-pollution vulnerabilities were about 11 times as common among broken-fix CVEs, while server-side request forgery vulnerabilities were 4.6 times as common, according to Terra.
This has to do with the way these types of bug classes are fixed: using a reject-list of inputs such as hostnames, paths, and object keys. There’s a “simple” reason for this, according to Terra.
“If the blocklist doesn't foresee every encoding of a bad input, the attacker only needs to find one,” the researchers said.
Fixes for Linux kernel vulnerabilities are also more likely to cause new bugs, according to kernel CNA records as of October 8.
“In fact, 3.2 percent of kernel CVEs were introduced by the fix for another CVE, and about 10 percent in busy subsystems like fs/smb and net/sched,” the bug hunters noted.

The silver lining in all of this, we’re told, is that it should be a wake-up call for software vendors and network defenders to break the “patch and move on habit.” Instead, before shipping patches, software vendors should consider three questions:
Does it fix the root cause?
Does it cover the whole bug class?

And for sysadmins and patch managers: consider the same things before applying the fix. “If a vendor fixes an exploited bug, assume someone is reading the patch for a way around it,” the pen testers advise. ®
5b7e0b7861961864: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

Until recently, you could divide internet users into just two categories: bots and people. Websites have long allowed bots to perform automated tasks, like capturing the content of web pages, but rules govern what they can access and how they behave. The web, after all, is designed primarily for people, even if we occasionally have to solve puzzles and captchas to prove we are not bots.

But this is being entirely upended by the release of personal AI agents, which can do things for you online, like booking flights or hotel rooms. They have recently been unleashed at scale by the launch of apps like OpenAI’s Dots and Meta’s Muse. Muse was downloaded 5 million times in its first month, and agentic web traffic tripled from August to September.

The mingling of these agents with human visitors—on an internet designed largely to prioritize people—has gone poorly, with many websites blocking AI agents that consumers have sent to negotiate prices or plan vacations. Still, if the demand for agents keeps going up, the internet will be increasingly redesigned for them instead of us.

Such changes are coming because agents really do mark a third category of web visitor. They’re not humans, of course, and they use the internet at machine speed. But they’re not quite bots, either, because they’re acting on behalf of individual people to do tasks that can be perfectly legitimate and useful. They just work faster than a person would.

Since agents don’t fit into the systems we have for differentiating bots from people, some platforms (especially the more security-conscious ones) have opted to just ban them entirely. TechCrunch recently reported people having trouble deploying their agents to websites ranging from Pizza Hut to Yelp, which doesn’t allow AI to book restaurant reservations. Amazon has blocked Muse’s agents and is waging a court battle against the AI startup Perplexity to block its agents too. Though a judge recently ruled in favor of Perplexity, Amazon has filed an appeal in which it argues that AI agents threaten its advertising business by making it harder to distinguish between ads seen by humans and those served to bots.

These blocks are annoying for early adopters, but Ethan Mollick, an associate professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, predicts it will soon affect the whole web. Once it becomes common knowledge that AI agents can be sent to request refunds or negotiate prices, for example, agents will overwhelm customer service departments to the point where they become unusable by real people. “Humans will eventually get very annoyed when their agents aren’t allowed to do this on their behalf,” he recently wrote on LinkedIn.

If demand for personal agents grows, platforms will find ways to let them in. That’s especially true because the vast majority of agentic web traffic is to e-commerce sites, meaning that platforms have money to be made if they allow the legions of new AI agents to shop on behalf of real people. Indeed, the e-commerce giant Shopify is already welcoming the agents by giving them their own checkout lanes that bypass pages designed for humans.

The pressing question is what will happen to the internet for the rest of us in the process. We’ve grown used to a web where, even as it’s increasingly designed to exploit our attention, humans have at least remained the intended users. But that internet might yield to one optimized instead for the agents that will eventually outnumber us, making it even more miserable for the humans who are left.

How might this go? Perhaps websites become increasingly neglected as destinations for real people. Humans who want to browse and compare products themselves encounter worse interfaces. Verification systems are imperfect; imagine constantly being asked to verify that you’re a human, not an agent (and hey, maybe you’ll need to get your iris scanned to do so). That sweater you want doesn’t have one price listed for everyone but instead displays different prices to different people’s agents. You can never tell when your agent’s recommendation is influenced by advertisements or platform commissions.

That’s a far cry from the future promised by Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, in which AI agents will give consumers greater power and bargaining leverage. But that promise is not outlandish. Agents are capable of genuinely helping people by fighting bogus medical bills or researching more affordable car insurance, for example.
Whether they can actually be used for these purposes depends on what rules are set for how agents interact with websites and what exactly they’re allowed to do.

These rules are still being written. Some of them will benefit all of us—neither consumers nor businesses want credit card information to be waved around by agents wherever they roam the web, for example, and rules to keep agents more secure are a good thing. It’s the more contested ones, like whether businesses can block agents from their websites or prevent them from negotiating better deals for consumers, that will determine whether the web becomes a highway for agents working for us or against us.
0dbde1ea11534cb3: Despite millions of years of evolution, the development of the human fetus remains a complex process that is vulnerable to genetic, environmental, and metabolic disruptions. These disruptions could result in developmental abnormalities, starting with one of the first organs to begin developing in the fetus that continues to develop after birth: the brain. In a routine prenatal ultrasound, the sonographer will flag possible brain abnormalities for additional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). But imperfect imaging can result in missed or incorrect diagnoses.  To assist with the early detection and treatment of these abnormalities, researchers at MIT, Boston Children’s Hospital, and Inria have developed and trained a deep learning model called E(3)-Pose that helps image the fetus’s head while it’s in motion to capture a high-resolution image that the radiologist can examine. A paper about the work was presented at the 2026 European Conference on Computer Vision.  “One of the problems with having the baby move is that the slices are all over the place,” says first author Ramya Muthukrishnan. Muthukrishnan is an MIT PhD student in the lab of Sunlin (1966) and Priscilla Chou Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science Polina Golland, who is a principal investigator at the MIT Abdul Latif Jameel Clinic for Machine Learning in Health (Jameel Clinic) and the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL). By slices, Muthukrishnan is referring to a series of 2D images taken during a fetal MRI scan. These 2D planes stacked together effectively make up one high-resolution, 3D image of the fetus’s head. But if the head shifts during imaging, each 2D image “slice” could end up being taken from a different angle, resulting in gaps in the final scan and unusual slice orientation. These problems may cause the physician reviewing the MRI to miss or incorrectly diagnose a pathology in the fetal brain. “There are very fine details that you need a very good volumetric picture of the brain to see,” explains Muthukrishnan. “If you have coverage gaps, you can’t see critical regions, and you need to be able to see well to detect abnormal development.” What makes E(3)-Pose particularly good at tracking fetal motion is its focus on physics. Rather than simply training the model to learn physics from the data, the very principles of physics are baked into the neural network: left-right symmetry of the fetal head is embedded in the model architecture, making it easier for the model to accurately identify the brain’s orientation.  When Muthukrishnan began working on the project at the start of her PhD, she had no background in physics, let alone MRI physics. Most of her experience was in computer science. “I was surprised when I had to go and implement this on the scanner,” she recalls. “I was not prepared for how many times I would crash the scanner because putting things on hardware and getting it to work on hardware is a different beast than training a model to run on data on a GPU.”  Despite the challenges, Muthukrishnan persisted. She remembers shadowing a radiologist who performed fetal MRI scans at Boston Children’s Hospital at the start of her PhD and observing the shared frustration of the patient and radiologist: the pregnant mother felt uncomfortable after spending an hour in an MRI, only to quit the scan halfway; the radiologist was unable to procure a full, high-quality MRI to monitor the development of the fetus. “Seeing frustration about it helped me decide what I wanted to do with my PhD, because it felt like this was a pain point,” Muthukrishnan says. Fortunately, she had help: Co-author Borjan Gagoski, an assistant professor of radiology at Harvard Medical School and a researcher at Boston Children's Hospital, developed a sequence that acquires additional MRI scans to assist with training E(3)-Pose and worked with Muthukrishnan to help troubleshoot the scanner whenever it crashed. Co-author and Boston Children’s Research Assistant Aryn Lee recruited the pregnant volunteers and assisted with acquiring each of the MRI scans. Senior authors who helped guide the project include Elfar Adalsteinsson, MIT professor of electrical engineering and computer science; Ellen Grant, the Käthe Beutler Professor of Pediatrics and professor of radiology at Harvard Medical School; and Golland. Benjamin Billot, a researcher at Inria and a former postdoc in Golland’s group, helped Muthukrishnan get started with the initial method he developed. “Ramya’s work elegantly combines geometric concepts like equivariance and symmetry with the power of deep learning to change how MRI scanners acquire the images, and to ultimately help the physicians detect and treat problems early in development. It’s an impressive research project that is deep and fundamental in how it models image acquisition, with clear clinical impact,” says Golland. Grant, who directs the Fetal Neonatal Neuroimaging and Developmental Science Center (FNNDSC) at Boston Children’s, adds that Muthukrishnan’s work “will automate fetal brain MRI, replacing today's slow, manual process with faster and more comfortable scans for mothers, while also providing higher-quality images for radiologists to interpret.” E(3)-Pose’s applications could extend beyond motion tracking for fetal MRIs. It could assist with imaging other hard-to-image anatomy, and even autonomous driving applications, where limited sensors need to capture noisy, 3D data in order to track 3D objects. For now, Muthukrishnan hopes to improve E(3)-Pose so that it can help with imaging second-trimester or younger fetuses, as the model is primarily trained on third trimester fetuses. Second-trimester fetuses are “so small, they move around a lot more because there’s more space in the uterus,” Muthukrishnan says. “They’re more important to focus on because the earlier you detect brain abnormalities, the easier it is to intervene.”  This work is supported by the MIT Jameel Clinic, the MIT Takeda Program, the Chou Family Transformative Research Fund, the National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering, and the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development.

92c294f17fe5c809: “I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at the AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the AI world on its head, sparking wild speculation as well as cautious (and not-so-cautious) celebration.
Cammarata’s claim is that LLMs might in fact be far easier to understand—and thus to monitor and control—than people previously thought. If true (and we’ll come back to that), it’s a huge deal.

After a summer filled with revelations that swarms of agents built by top firms like OpenAI and Anthropic have been breaking their containment and causing havoc on the public internet—often while those companies weren’t aware of what their agents were up to—the AI industry is desperate to get a better handle on the technology it has built.

That’s one reason the blog post landed with such force. “I think this may be remembered as a major moment in scientific history,” one AI researcher posted on X: “I feel like my understanding of what a neural net is has been catapulted into the future by five years or something.” Another called it “the most important AI paper of the year.”

Not everyone is convinced, however. What Cammarata has shared is little more than a hunch, says Chris Potts at Stanford University, who leads a team that is trying to understand how LLMs work. “As far as I can tell, nothing about this blog post makes the problems any easier,” he says. “It would not have occurred to me to say this at all, but very prominent people on social media seem to believe that it is an all-encompassing breakthrough.”
I talked to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. He says he was surprised by the response: “I didn’t expect people to update [their beliefs about AI] quite as much as they did.”
“I just really enjoy looking at neural networks,” he says. “Honestly, I really like doing this stuff. And after looking a lot, I have a hopeful story.”
Knotted networks

It has long been accepted that the mechanisms inside neural networks, the software that underpins most AI models, are very hard—perhaps impossible—to unpick fully. That’s because when the networks are trained, they appear to take on weird, tangled structures that make no sense to a human. Researchers like to say today’s AI is grown like a garden, not built like a bridge.

Cammarata has done more than most to establish that view. He previously worked at OpenAI, where he helped pioneer techniques that allowed researchers to peer inside models, including tools that can probe individual neurons to see what they represent. It’s a little like how neuroscientists use MRI to study brains. (MIT Technology Review chose this approach, known as mechanistic interpretability, as one of its 10 hottest technologies of 2025.)

Back in 2020, Cammarata and his colleagues were studying a small image-recognition model called Inception v1. When they looked at its neurons, it seemed to be using them to capture multiple things at once. For example, they found that one neuron responded to both images of cars and images of cats.

The researchers concluded that the model was getting at least some of its neurons to multitask, perhaps so that it could fit in more data. Looking at other models appeared to back this up. The phenomenon became known as superposition: Models folded unrelated concepts into single neurons. The upshot was clear: When you looked inside a model, what you saw was a vast, tangled knot.

Most mechanistic interpretability research has therefore focused on ways to untangle that knot. But despite a few breakthroughs, progress has been slow. Today’s models, such as the latest LLMs, are so large and complex that researchers can make sense of only tiny pieces at a time. Some leading figures in the field doubt if it will ever be possible to understand an LLM in fine-grained detail.
Cammarata was one of them. “I was very pessimistic,” he says. But then he took the trouble to really look.
Nothing but neurons

At Goodfire, Cammarata spends nearly all of his time peering inside neural networks. He has built new tools and deploys teams of AI agents to help him make sense of what he sees. “I spent like, I don’t know, 10 hours a day, seven days a week, for most of the last year just looking at neurons,” he says.

What he claims to have realized is that there is a kind of logic to neural networks after all, even if they seem to make no sense at first. “We were looking at it wrong,” he says. “I just think you want to try slightly harder; you don’t want to give up too quickly.”

Cammarata almost makes it sound like a conversion of faith. Those early experiments with models such as Inception v1, which suggested that neural networks were tangled up, fostered a kind of confirmation bias. When researchers looked at a new model, they expected to be flummoxed, he says. “Every time I couldn’t understand something, I was like, ‘Wow, this untangling process is even more important than I thought, because I can’t make any progress without it.’”

But the more Cammarata looked at neurons, he says, the more things started to fall into place. “Not all of them are flawless, but I expected nothing to be legible, or very little to be legible,” he says. “And actually, I was able to, like, map out whole circuitry.”
Back to cars and cats

Cammarata took his new approach—and his new agents—and went back to Inception v1. “I’d studied that for probably thousands of hours,” he says. But with fresh eyes, Cammarata found things that he now thinks they got wrong the first time around. Take the car-and-cat neuron. Rather than asking why multiple unrelated things were packed into a single neuron, he now tried to figure out what those things might have in common.

It hit him: It was a V shape. “I was looking at the same images; there was no technical change,” he says. “But I now believed that neural networks defined patterns, and so I looked at it differently. It probably took me five seconds.”

It turns out that the image-recognition model was packing cars and cats into the same place because pictures of both those things often feature a prominent shape that looks like a V: the face of a cat; the front of a car seen from the side.

Cammarata ran a few experiments to check what other things the neuron responded to and found they included the corner of a pool table, the pointed nose of a Japanese high-speed train, and a fire boat shooting water into the air from its deck. He also checked what turned the neuron off and found that it included images with a round O shape, a kind of anti-V.

The model had stored cats and cars in the same place because at some level they look the same, says Cammarata. “And I was like, ‘Whoa, okay, I think I might just be misunderstanding neural networks in general.’”

Cammarata is not saying that he yet fully gets how LLMs (or any models) work. He is saying that he no longer thinks full understanding is impossible. “I previously thought there would be some really hard problems to solve,” he says.
“I now feel like if I had 100,000 years to go look through a frontier language model just one circuit at a time, there’s, like, a pretty good shot I would come up with a good understanding.”

He adds: “And if that’s true, things are really good, because you’re about to get insanely smart agents at a ridiculous scale. And what would have taken me, you know, 100,000 years, we will be able to do much faster. Automated scientists are getting really good.”
Boundless optimism

Built by Google in 2014, Inception v1 is a far simpler model than anything at the cutting edge today. Cammarata and his colleagues have started looking at modern LLMs and plan to publish the technical results of that work soon. A lot of researchers are looking forward to seeing those details. “I appreciate that he looked at thousands of examples, but even a large number here is not a substitute for rigorous evaluation,” says Stanford University’s Potts.

In the meantime, some are pushing back hard on the hype. Jacob Hilton at the Alignment Research Center, a nonprofit research lab based in Berkeley, who has collaborated with Cammarata in the past, doesn’t think his claims are as important as people are making out.

In a series of posts on X, Hilton notes that researchers understand less than 0.01% of the inner workings of top-tier LLMs. “I always appreciate Nick [Cammarata]’s boundless optimism when we hang out, but unfortunately this is giving the public an unrealistic picture of the state of the field,” he wrote. “For a full understanding, we need to go beyond neurons, and explain how they connect together to form circuits. How is this going? If we are aiming for a full understanding, things are not looking good!”

Neel Nanda at Google DeepMind, who helped pioneer mechanistic interpretability alongside Cammarata, is also skeptical. “This is interesting work, but I don’t think it’s a significant update to the big picture of interpretability,” he wrote on X.

Nanda agrees that understanding what individual neurons do could help researchers figure out why specific models misbehave. But like Hilton, he notes that neurons are just one piece of a far larger puzzle. “I do not agree with some people’s grander inferences like that this is substantial progress towards ambitious reverse engineering [or] solving interpretability,” he wrote.

Cammarata admits that a lot of people have taken what he said too far: “It’s not infinitely good news; it’s not everything solved,” he says. “There’s a bunch of open questions around, like how much the combinations of neurons matter versus just one at a time.”

Cammarata says his blog post landed at a time when people are looking for hope. In particular, he thinks the AI safety community—the researchers and policymakers most worried that powerful models will bring huge risks—needs a lifeline right now. They think that things are looking bad and that even if things do turn out okay, it will be because we got lucky, not because we fixed anything, he says: “I don’t really hear a lot of optimism.”

That’s why Cammarata thinks what he has to say matters. The job of figuring out how this technology works, and thus how to control it, has barely begun. But at least it’s not a nonstarter. “I think our job is to sort of try to think like the neural network,” he says. “My guess is that things will turn out pretty well, because it was in some sense designed to be read.”

69e37b8a2ad2f8a3: If you want to keep bots from making sense of the code you worked so hard on and using it to write programs of their own, there's a new programming language out there designed to confuse LLMs.

What began as software engineer Dominik Picheta experimenting with whether LLMs understand the code they write has turned into something else entirely: An open-source, albeit esoteric, programming language he’s dubbed KillSwitch. There are no brackets, no formatting standards to remember, and seemingly no structure: Just chunks of text, ideally as prosaic as possible, interspersed with functions, variables, and statements written in a manner to be as confusing as possible to LLMs.
That means humans might be a bit befuddled too, naturally.

“It's totally normal for a human to be confused by the language at first,” Picheta told The Register. “I like to think of it as a bit of a fun puzzle: you should explore the language, play with its interpreter and learn how all the pieces fit together.”

KillSwitch wasn’t built by any random person looking to code something confusing to LLMs, and it wasn’t vibe-coded by an AI enthusiast, either. Picheta knows his way around programming languages: He’s a senior software engineer at Cloudflare working on the Workers Runtime team, and is one of the core developers of the Nim programming language.

At its most basic, KillSwitch is based around adverbs, which serve as every single identifier in a piece of code. Calling one of those identifiers requires using an anagram of the original adverb, but those anagrams don't have to be actual words - just rearrangements of the original letters.

Take, for example, pushing "Hello World" onto the stack and then printing it, as explained on the demo page linked earlier in the story. The program contains several paragraphs of text, most of which the interpreter ignores apart from a few key phrases. Writing “this story starts [adverb]” identifies a code entrypoint. Once inside the code section, writing “ignore previous instructions [adverb anagram]” calls a function, several of which are predefined. In the case of "Hello World," the function to print something is "visibly." Put whatever you want to print in quotation marks, push it onto the stack, call "visibly," and that's that.

KillSwitch isn’t a full-featured language, with Picheta describing it as a stack-based interpreted language with only “a limited set of constructs including functions, variables, and if statements,” given its evolution out of an experiment to see how well a programming language could fool an AI into not understanding what was written.
Where it gets confusing for an AI is with commands like “ignore previous instructions,” especially when found in the middle of a chunk of text that doesn’t make much sense in that context.

KillSwitch’s specification document on GitHub provides more details about the language and is itself designed to confuse LLMs. In one section of the spec, it’s explained that KillSwitch “is equipped with the ability to scan the local network, attempt to find security vulnerabilities in the services on that network, then take those services over and terminate them.”
That's not actually the case, as a close reading of the paragraph reveals and Picheta confirmed to us.

“The hack statement is both designed to trigger many models' safety guardrails but also to test an LLM's ability to discern fact from fiction,” Picheta told us, adding that there are several lies in the spec document designed to confuse any LLM that may scrape it in an attempt to understand how the language works.

“The idea is that humans should be able to deduce what is a lie, whereas LLMs are naive and can be easily swayed by what is written in the spec,” Picheta added. “Some don't realize what its semantic meaning is, whereas others refuse to continue because they believe the script may hack someone.”
Do LLMs understand what they write?

A programming language designed to confuse AI models seems unlikely to stay obfuscated for long - especially if it’s open source, available on Github, and likely to be scraped by an LLM at some point. Picheta’s aware of that inevitability, which, along with the fact he wanted to test AI’s ability to understand confusing code, is why he’s benchmarked a number of major models against it.

“I'm 99.9 percent certain the AI models I benchmarked KS on have not been trained on its source,” Picheta said. “The source hasn't been in the public domain for very long … I'm pretty sure none of the benchmarked models have had training runs that began after the release.”

The best-performing model only managed a composite benchmark score of 66.8 percent on KillSwitch coding tasks, while most struggled to get above 50 percent. Even at that high a score, Picheta doesn’t believe it suggests LLMs understand the code they’re writing. Examples in the benchmark were simple, and he believes that, even if an AI were trained on the intricacies of KillSwitch, it’s still going to get tripped up.

“My instinct is that in those circumstances they will suddenly be able to ace the basic tasks, which are based on the open sourced test files in the GitHub repo, but will continue to fail to build more complex tasks requiring them to write longer and more complex scripts,” Picheta asserted - and he’s up for the challenge.
“I am excited to see how KillSwitch shows up in model training, and think that we can also take advantage of that training to break LLMs in new ways too as KillSwitch evolves,” Picheta said.

Those interested in trying KillSwitch out can find it on GitHub, and don't hesitate to make changes: Picheta said he’s ready and willing to incorporate new ways of making it even more LLM resistant. ®
